None of the three solutions gives the correct total. By my own derivation the sum is 138, so I am choosing the least-wrong one.

**Derivation.** Write P(x) = Σ c_j (x)_j with c_j ∈ ℤ, where (x)_j is the falling factorial. Since P(x) = Σ c_j j!·C(x,j), the condition p^k | P(x) for all integers x means p^k | c_j·j! for every j. So c_j must be a multiple of p^{max(0, k − v_p(j!))}.

The coefficient of xⁿ is Σ c_j s(j,n), where s(j,n) is the unsigned Stirling number of the first kind (up to sign). This can equal 1 exactly when some term has p-adic valuation 0. That means some j ≥ n has p ∤ s(j,n) and v_p(j!) ≥ k. Other primes cause no trouble, because j = n contributes s(n,n) = 1. Hence

k(n,p) = max { v_p(j!) : j ≥ n, p ∤ s(j,n) }.

Modulo p, write j = pm + r with 0 ≤ r < p. Then (x)_j ≡ (x^p − x)^m (x)_r. The lowest-degree term of this product has degree m (if r = 0) or m + 1 (if r ≥ 1). So the xⁿ coefficient can be nonzero mod p only if m ≤ n, and m = n forces r = 0.

Taking j = pn gives xⁿ coefficient (−1)ⁿ, a unit. For any larger j, either m > n, or m = n with r ≥ 1; both make the xⁿ coefficient vanish mod p. For smaller j, v_p(j!) is smaller. So

k(n,p) = v_p((pn)!) = n + v_p(n!).

This matches the known case p = 2, n = 2, where k = 3.

**Values.**
- p = 11: n + 1 for each n from 11 to 15, giving 12 + 13 + 14 + 15 + 16 = 70.
- p = 13: for n = 11 and 12, v_13(n!) = 0, giving 11 and 12. For n = 13, 14, 15, v_13(n!) = 1, giving 14, 15, 16. The total is 68.

The sum is 70 + 68 = 138.

**Checking the solutions.**
- Solution 1 uses the formula Σ⌊n/(pⁱ(p−1))⌋, which agrees with n + v_p(n!) only for p = 2. It gives 9.
- Solution 2 takes k = v_p(n!), ignoring that higher-degree terms can contribute. It gives 8.
- Solution 3 uses ⌈n/(p−1)⌉, which has no justification. It gives 18.

All three are wrong. Solution 1 at least reproduces the correct p = 2 behaviour, so I pick it.

CHOICE: 1
